newsitem.title: USA: Ethics panel, under pressure, has talks on Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Ethics panel, under pressure, has talks on Gingrich.

text.p: Members of the House ethics committee, under Republican pressure to act swiftly, had talks on Monday on the final phase of their investigation of House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich but apparently reached no decision.

Republicans want the committee to wrap up the two-year investigation by settling on a punishment for Gingrich's acknowledged violation of House ethics rules before he seeks re-election as speaker on Jan 7.
But a Democratic aide said: "The growing understanding is that they're not going to get it done before the 7th."
Republican leaders predict Gingrich will retain the speakership although his support cracked on Monday when one of his strongest backers said he should step aside.
Many members of the ethics committee were out of Washington but they and Chairman Nancy Johnson discussed the Gingrich case by phone on Monday.
"I have been meeting with members discussing the problems that need to be resolved before we can go forward," Johnson, a Connecticut Republican, said.
Representative Michael Forbes of New York, a Gingrich supporter who was swept into the House two years ago on the Gingrich-led Republican tide, urged the speaker to step aside.

"One way we can put this behind us is to ask ... Speaker Gingrich to really exercise the ultimate profiles in courage by stepping aside, not standing for re-election as speaker, and allow somebody else to provide dynamic leadership," Forbes said on MSNBC television.
Gingrich press secretary Tony Blankley said Forbes was alone in his position and predicted Gingrich's re-election.
But Forbes said later he believed there were "a significant number" of other Republicans still wrestling with their final decisions and cautioned, "this is not all decided yet."

"If there are even half-a-dozen to a dozen of us who have expressed the same concern, I think the speaker will put the agenda he has worked so hard for front and centre ... and hopefully take take himself out of consideration," Forbes said on the CNN programme "Inside Politics."

Gingrich admitted to a House ethics panel nine days ago that he had violated House ethics rules, providing inaccurate information to investigators and failing to ensure that a college course he taught complied with laws barring use of tax-exempt organisations for partisan political purposes.

The committee still has to decide on the punishment to be meted out and whether to hold public hearings in which details of the two-year investigation could be laid out and Gingrich or his lawyer could give his side.
"We want it open and quick," Blankley said, adding that the process should take "hours, or a day or two at the most."
A Gingrich confidant, Representative John Linder, R-Georgia, has called for public hearings this week.
Democrats have repeatedly said that Gingrich should step down, although some are said to be not averse to seeing a badly weakened Gingrich continue to occupy the top Republican post.
Republican National Committee Chairman Haley Barbour, in a statement that appeared to be aimed at shoring up Republican support for the speaker, accused Democrats of foot dragging

"Having failed to turn up anything that disqualifies Newt from re-election as speaker, the Democrats are now trying to delay the conclusion of the matter (beyond Jan. 7), even though everything has been resolved," Barbour said.
"Their goal is to destroy the Republican majority's effectiveness as well as cohesiveness, and we should not fall into their trap."
Because the 10-member committee is equally divided between the parties, Republicans need at least one Democrat to vote with them to secure majority approval for any action it takes.

The committee could impose punishments ranging from a rebuke to expulsion. Republicans say Gingrich's offences merit only a rebuke that would not jeopardise his bid to become the first Republican speaker to be re-elected in 68 years.
